result.markdown: --- title: "Accessible Data Representations" author: "Mine Doğucu" execute: echo: true format: revealjs: menu: openButton: false footer: | [stat-100.com](https://stat-100.com) code-line-numbers: false slide-number: true incremental: false theme: [default, style.scss] logo: path: images/00-stat100-logo-square.png alt: "STAT 100 course square logo" transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: "images/stat100-logo-rectangle.png" data-background-size: 10% data-background-position: 50% 85% data-aria-label: "STAT 100 course logo" --- # Improving Data Visualizations {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ::: {.cell} ::: ## Packages for Today ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(hellodatascience) library(tidyverse) ``` ::: ## Saving a Plot ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} base_bar_plot <- ggplot( data = atus_college, aes( x = employment, fill = enrollment ) ) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") base_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Side-by-side bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-base-bar-plot-1.png){#fig-base-bar-plot fig-alt='Grouped bar chart showing student counts by employment status and enrollment. The x-axis, labeled \'employment\', lists employment categories (Full Time, Part Time, NA) and the y-axis, labeled \'count\' shows count. Bars are colored by enrollment status (Full Time vs Part Time), allowing comparison of enrollment within each employment group.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Labels ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} improved_bar_plot <- base_bar_plot + labs( # <1> title = "Student Count by Employment and Enrollment Status", # <2> subtitle = "Most students work part-time while enrolled full-time", # <3> x = "Employment Status", # <4> y = "Number of Students", # <5> fill = "Course Enrollment", # <6> caption = "Data source: American Time Use Survey 2024 (n = 312 students)" # <7> ) improved_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status with added labels](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-labs-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-labs fig-alt='Same bar chart as previous with better labels. The main title is Student Count by Employment and Enrollment and the subtitle says that most students work part-time while enrolled full-time. Labels for the x-axis, y-axis, and legend are \'Employment Status\', \'Number of Students\' and \'Course Enrollment\' respectively. Caption notes Data source: American Time Use Survey 2024 (n = 321 students). There are more students enrolled full time than part time for each level of employment status. The full time enrolled students with unknown employment status have the highest count at about 80 students. ' width=960} ::: ::: ## Themes ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} improved_bar_plot <- improved_bar_plot + theme_minimal() improved_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status with using `theme_minimal`](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-themes-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-themes fig-alt='Same bar chart as previous, with a white background instead of gray.' width=960} ::: ::: Other themes include but not limited to: `theme_bw()`, `theme_light()`, `theme_dark()`, `theme_classic()`. ## Using `theme()` function ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} improved_bar_plot <- improved_bar_plot + theme( # <1> plot.title = element_text(size = 18), # <2> plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14), axis.title = element_text(size = 12), axis.text = element_text(size = 10), legend.title = element_text(size = 11), legend.text = element_text(size = 9), plot.caption = element_text(size = 8) ) + labs(title = "Student Count by Employment and \n Enrollment Status") # <3> improved_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status with bigger font sizes](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-font-size-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-font-size fig-alt='Same bar plot as previous with larger font size and title broken across two lines.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Changing legend location ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} improved_bar_plot <- improved_bar_plot + theme(legend.position = "bottom") # <1> improved_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status with legend at the bottom](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-legend-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-legend fig-alt='Same plot as previous with legend horizontally listed at bottom of plot instead of vertically listed on right side of plot.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Colors ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Nine colors randomly selected from R colors as listed by the `colors()` function](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-colors-1.png){#fig-colors fig-alt='Color palette display arranged in a 3-by-3 grid of colored squares. Each square is labeled with a named color, including lightcyan3, grey25, peachpuff, chartreuse3, khaki1, hotpink, cornsilk2, lavenderblush, and purple3.' width=960} ::: ::: [Colors in R full list](https://r-charts.com/colors/) ## Hex Codes ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Hex codes for the randomly selected nine colors](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-hex-1.png){#fig-hex fig-alt='Color palette grid showing nine colored squares, each labeled with its hexadecimal color code, including #B4CDCD, #404040, #FFDAB9, #66CD00, #FFF68F, #FF69B4, #EEE8CD, #FFF0F5, and #7D26CD.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Okabe-Ito Color Palette ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "#000000" "#E69F00" "#56B4E9" "#009E73" "#F0E442" "#0072B2" "#D55E00" [8] "#CC79A7" "#999999" ``` ::: ::: ## Okabe-Ito Color Palette ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Hex codes of colors in the Okabe-Ito palette](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-okabe-ito-1.png){#fig-okabe-ito fig-alt='Three-by-three grid of color swatches labeled with hexadecimal codes, including #000000 (black), #E69F00 (gold), #56B4E9 (light blue), #009E73 (teal), #F0E442 (yellow), #0072B2 (dark blue), #D55E00 (orange), #CC79A7 (pink), and #999999 (gray), intended as a reference color palette.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Changing Colors ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} improved_bar_plot <- improved_bar_plot + scale_fill_manual( # <1> values = c( # <2> "Full Time" = "#009E73", # <3> "Part Time" = "#CC79A7" # <4> ) ) improved_bar_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status using Okabe-Ito colors](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-okabe-colors-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-okabe-colors fig-alt='Most recent bar plot with different colors chosen for the bars.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Look at how far we have come - Default plot ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Default Bar Plot](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-recall-base-bar-plot-1.png){#fig-recall-base-bar-plot fig-alt='Original first bar plot from beginning of the chapter.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Look at how far we have come - Improved plot ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Improved Bar plot](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-okabe-colors-again-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-okabe-colors-again fig-alt='Most recent bar plot with different colors chosen for the bars.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Customizing Scatterplots ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} simple_scatterplot <- ggplot( data = atus_college, aes( x = time_alone, y = weekly_earnings ) ) + geom_point() + labs( x = "Time Alone (minutes)", y = "Weekly Earnings ($)" ) + theme_bw() simple_scatterplot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Scatterplot of time spent alone and weekly earnings](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-scatterplot-1.png){#fig-scatterplot fig-alt='Scatter plot showing the relationship between time spent alone and weekly earnings. Each point represents an individual. Time alone (in minutes) is on the x-axis and weekly earnings are on the y-axis. Earnings vary widely at all levels of time alone, with no strong linear trend.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Customizing Scatterplots ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} colored_scatterplot <- simple_scatterplot + geom_point( color = "aquamarine4", # <1> size = 4, # <2> shape = "square" # <3> ) colored_scatterplot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Scatterplot with customized appearance of points](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-scatterplot-look-1.png){#fig-scatterplot-look fig-alt='Same scatterplot as previous with points as green squares instead of black circles.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Facets ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simple_scatterplot + facet_grid(rows = vars(employment), cols = vars(enrollment)) # <1> ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time spent alone versus weekly earnings broken by employment and enrollment status using facets](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-scatterplot-facet-1.png){#fig-scatterplot-facet fig-alt='Faceted version of same scatter plot of weekly earnings versus time alone, split by employment status (Full Time, Part Time, and NA). Each panel shows individual data points, allowing comparison of earnings patterns within each employment group. There are no obvious trends in either Full Time Enrollment plot. The part time employment plots are mostly weekly earnings between 0 and 1000$. The NA employment plots are empty.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Facets - Rows only ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simple_scatterplot + facet_grid(rows = vars(employment)) # <1> ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Time spent alone versus weekly earnings broken by employment status](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-scatterplot-facet-employ-1.png){#fig-scatterplot-facet-employ fig-alt='Vertical faceted scatter plot of same data showing weekly earnings versus time alone for three employment categories: Full Time, Part Time, and NA. Full-time workers tend to have higher earnings overall, while part-time workers cluster at lower earnings levels.' width=960} ::: ::: # Data Verbalization {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ## Screen Readers An assistive technology is any form of technology (software, device) that helps people with disabilities perform certain activities (e.g. walking sticks, wheel chairs). . . . A screen reader is a form of assistive technology that allows blind and visually impaired users, and people with other disabilities (e.g., dyslexia) to read what is on their computer screen. . . . If you have never heard of a screen reader reading a text, you can listen to [this audio](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l-G4kKTuDHI&t=2s). ## Alternate (alt) Text A screen reader can read text, but non-text elements such as images cannot be read. . . . Instead a screen reader would say something along the lines of "Image.png". . . . In order to make an image visually accessible, we can rely on alternate text. Alternate text or alt text describes contents of an image and can be read by screen readers. ## Alt text in ggplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code .code-overflow-wrap} improved_bar_plot + labs( alt = "Barplot showing student count by employment and enrollment status. The y-axis shows number of students from 0 to 80, and the x-axis shows employment status (Full Time, Part Time, NA). Each employment status is broken down by full time or part time enrollment status. The plot displays six bars: students enrolled full time with full time employment (approximately 70 students), part time employment (apprximately 75 students), and unknown employment (approximately 80 students) as well as students enrolled part time with full time employment (approxmately 60 students), part time employment (approximately 18 students), and unknown employment (approximately 15 students). Data source: American Time Use Survey 2024 (n = 312 students)." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of employment broken down by enrollment status with added alternative text in the background](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-bar-plot-alt-1.png){#fig-bar-plot-alt fig-alt='Same well polished bar plot of employment status by course enrollment.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Alt text is invisible The alt text is never displayed in the front end. . . . The alt text is stored on the back end of a web page and is legible by screen readers. . . . If you are reading these slides using a screen reader, you should hear the alt text for the plot in the previous slide. ## Good alt text practice You should always write alt text for all images (ggplot or not), whether you use R or Quarto or not, whether you are doing work for STAT 100 or any other courses or any non-course work. . . . An effective alt text communicates the labels of the axes, the variables represented, ranges and values for each variable and group as seen in the visualization. ## Good alt text practice Most importantly alt text should convey the overall message of the visualization. . . . Writing the overall message of the visualization is crucial and practicing this skill will help you take the time to understand the visualizations you work with in depth. # Data Sonification {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ## Saving Simple Plot ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1:10 y <- 1:10 simple_plot <- ggplot( data = data.frame(x = x, y = y), aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() simple_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simple scatterplot to show how `sonify()` function works](03b-represent-data_files/figure-revealjs/fig-simple-scatterplot-1.png){#fig-simple-scatterplot fig-alt='Simple scatter plot showing a perfectly positive linear relationship between x and y. Points increase steadily from lower left to upper right, indicating that y increases as x increases.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Sonification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sonify::sonify(x, y) ``` ::: If you were to listen to the output of the `sonify()` function, you would hear a series of ten tones, each one slightly higher in pitch than the last. The rising pitch directly corresponds to the rising `y` values as `x` increases. # Data Tactualization {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ## Data Tactualization Data tactualization refers to making data visualization in a form so that it can be touchable. The video shows printing of a tactile boxplot that one can touch using a Swell machine.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
